title: 2 Chronicles 11:18–23
context: This unit, without a parallel in Kings, describes Rehoboam’s family. His wives include Mahalath, of David’s family on both sides, and Maacah, called here the granddaughter of Absalom. Rehoboam has eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he chooses Abijah, Maacah’s son, as his heir. He places his sons in the fortified cities and provides for them. Maacah’s parentage is given differently in other places: 1 Kings 15:2 calls Abijam’s mother “Maacah the daughter of Abishalom,” and 2 Chronicles 13:2 calls Abijah’s mother “Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah.” The text does not explain the relationship between these notices, and this page does not harmonize them. Both traditions read the unit as historical description, without praising Rehoboam’s many marriages, and note the Chronicler’s comment that he “dealt wisely” in administering his sons.

verses.text: Rehoboam took a wife for himself, Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam marries Mahalath, of David’s family on both her father’s and her mother’s side. Arminian readers note the Chronicler’s attention to the royal family’s connection with David. The marriage strengthens Rehoboam’s ties to the house of David and Jesse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the emphasis on Davidic descent. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical description of a royal marriage, and both note that the Chronicler records it without moral comment.

verses.text: She bore him sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
verses.arminianNotes: Mahalath bears Rehoboam three sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham. Arminian readers note that the family record continues with the names of the king’s children. The record preserves them, although none becomes prominent later.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as straightforward family history. Shared ground: both traditions treat it as genealogical detail without doctrinal controversy, and see in it the Chronicler’s concern for the continuity of David’s house.

verses.text: After her, he took Maacah the granddaughter of Absalom; and she bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam then marries Maacah, granddaughter of Absalom, who bears Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith. Arminian readers note that Maacah’s son Abijah will become king. Other notices give her parentage differently, as the context records without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the importance of Maacah’s line for the succession and treat the differing notices with restraint. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as family history that prepares for Abijah’s reign, and neither builds conclusions on her exact parentage.

verses.text: Rehoboam loved Maacah the granddaughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines; for he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and became the father of twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam loves Maacah above all his wives and concubines, and he has eighteen wives, sixty concubines, twenty-eight sons, and sixty daughters. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler reports the facts without approval. A large harem recalls Solomon’s example and its dangers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the record as description, not endorsement, and recall the warning against a king multiplying wives (Deuteronomy 17:17). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical detail and decline to treat Rehoboam’s household as a model.

verses.text: Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah to be chief, the prince among his brothers, for he intended to make him king.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam appoints Abijah, Maacah’s son, as chief among his brothers, intending to make him king. Arminian readers note that the king exercises real choice in arranging the succession. His preference for Maacah shapes the future of Judah’s throne.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the king’s decision and see David’s line continuing through it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a historical account of succession, and neither finds a doctrinal question in Rehoboam’s choice of heir.

verses.text: He dealt wisely, and dispersed some of his sons throughout all the lands of Judah and Benjamin, to every fortified city. He gave them food in abundance; and he sought many wives for them.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam deals wisely, dispersing his sons among the fortified cities, giving them food in abundance and seeking wives for them. Arminian readers note the Chronicler’s commendation of his practical wisdom. He secures the kingdom by giving his sons roles and resources.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the description of Rehoboam acting wisely in administration. The arrangement may also have reduced rivalry over the throne, though the text does not say so. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as commending Rehoboam’s prudence while recognizing that 12:1 will tell a different story.
